 INTEREST OF AMICI CURIAE1
The NAACP Legal Defense and Educational
Fund, Inc. (“LDF”) is the nation’s first and foremost
civil rights organization. Since its founding in 1940,
LDF has fought to secure equal justice under the law
for all Americans, and to break down barriers that
prevent Black Americans from realizing their basic
civil and human rights.
Through litigation, advocacy, and public education,
LDF strives to enforce the United States
Constitution’s promise of equal protection and due
process for all. LDF has participated as counsel of
record in numerous significant cases before this Court
to de fend voting rights and challenge racial
discrimination in all its forms. See, e.g., Louisiana v.
Callais, 608 U.S. 85  (2026); Alexander v. South
Carolina State Conf. of the NAACP, 602 U.S. 1 (2024);
Allen v. Milligan, 599 U.S. 1 (2023); Buck v. Davis, 580
U.S. 100 (2017); Shelby Cnty. v. Holder, 570 U.S. 529

1 Pursuant to Supreme Court Rule 37.6, counsel for amici curiae
state that no counsel for a party before this Court authored this
brief in whole or in part and that no person other than amici
curiae, their members, or their counsel made a monetary
contribution to the preparation or submission of this brief.
Amicus the Lawyers’ Committee for Civil Rights under Law
states that it represents Native-American tribes and members in
the District Court proceedings in this case on an issue —
documentary proof of location of residence requirements —not
presented in  the Petitions.  The Lawyers’ Committee ’s clients
prevailed in the District Court, and there was no appeal from the
relief on their claims .  The Lawyers’ Committee has not
participated in the appellate proceedings in this case, including
before this Court.

2
(2013); Nw. Austin Mun. Dist. No. 1 v. Holder, 557 U.S.
193 (2009) ; Chisom v. Roemer , 501 U.S. 380 (1991);
Thornburg v. Gingles , 478 U.S. 30 (1986); City of
Mobile v. Bolden, 446 U.S. 55 (1980); Allen v. State Bd.
of Elections, 393 U.S. 544 (1969); Brown v. Bd. of Educ.
of Topeka, 347 U.S. 483 (1954). LDF has also resolved
litigation demonstrating violations of constitutional
and federal law on behalf of Black Americans in
binding judicial consent decrees. See, e.g., Chisom, 501
U.S. 380.
LDF is committed to ensuring a faithful
interpretation of federal voting laws and protecting
the right of every eligible Black American to cast a
ballot that counts on Election Day . LDF also has
extensive experience with judicial consent decrees ,
which have resolved needless litigation and ensured
compliance with federal anti-discrimination laws.
The National Association for the
Advancement of Colored People (“NAACP”)  is
the oldest and largest civil rights organization in the
United States. Founded in 1909 by pioneers of racial
justice, the NAACP’s core mission has long been to
ensure political, educational, social, and economic
equality.
In furtherance of its mission, the NAACP has
worked to protect the fundamental rights of its
members and all Black people and other people of
color, offering a unique slate of programs that provide
education, community -based advocacy, and general

3
assistance to voters seeking to make their voices
heard. For example, the NAACP develops and
executes programs that promote civic participation by
helping its members and other citizens register to vote
and aiding voters in casting their ballots. It also
supports its thousands of state, regional, and local
units working to advance the organization’s goals at
every level.
The NAACP’s efforts to advance its mission and
protect voters’ fundamental rights are undermined by
government actions that heighten barriers to voting.
The Lawyers’ Committee for Civil Rights
Under Law  is a nonpartisan, nonprofit civil rights
organization, formed at the request of President John
F. Kennedy in 1963, that uses legal advocacy to
achieve racial justice. For more than 60 years, the
Lawyers’ Committee has advocated inside and outside
the cour ts to ensure that Black people and other
people of color have the voice, opportunity, and power
to make the promises of democracy real. This includes
being able to gain unencumbered access to the ballot
and to remain on the ballot without being unfairly
purged. The Lawyers’ Committee litigates voting
rights cases across the country.
Many of these cases have given Black voters and
their communities the equal opportunity previously
denied them to participate in the political process. The
Lawyers’ Committee has litigated some of these voting
rights cases before this Court, including Shelby

4
County, 570 U.S. 529, Arizona v. Inter Tribal Council
of Arizona, Inc., 570 U.S. 1 (2013) (“ ITCA”), Young v.
Fordice, 520 U.S. 273 (1997), and Clark v. Roemer, 500
U.S. 646 (1991).
Through this litigation and other  advocacy, the
Lawyers’ Committee has challenged discriminatory
barriers to voter registration that have
disenfranchised Black people and other people of color,
as well as efforts to purge voters  of color  once they
have surmounted those barriers and made it onto the
voter rolls. Amici Curiae LDF, NAACP, and the
Lawyers’ Committee have a strong interest in the fair
application of the United States Constitution and
federal and state antidiscrimination laws . They
submit that their experience and knowledge will assist
the Court in this case.

5
INTRODUCTION AND SUMMARY OF THE
ARGUMENT

Congress enacted the National Voter Registration
Act of 1993 (“NVRA”  or “ Act”) under its Elections
Clause authority to “establish procedures that will
increase the number of eligible citizens who register to
vote in elections for Federal office,”  promote voter
registration procedures  that “enhance[] the
participation of eligible citizens as voters” in federal
elections, ensure the maintenance of “accurate and
current voter registration rolls,” and broadly “protect
the integrity of the electoral process .” 52 U.S.C. §
20501. Decades of evidence showed  that voter
registration practices as well as  periodic purge and
reregistration requirements often had the purpose and
effect of  disenfranchising eligible Black voters and
other voters of color. Congress thus prescribed precise
requirements for voter registration  forms and
prohibited all systematic purging of voter rolls within
90 days of any federal election.
Today, despite Congress’s effort to curb onerous
voter registration requirements and voter purges so
they would not disenfranchise eligible voters, states
continue to implement error-prone and discriminatory
programs that do just that. Numerous federal cou rts
have found that states’ attempts to institute
documentary proof of citizenship requirements and to
remove alleged non-citizens from the voter rolls yield

6
unfair and inaccurate results, thereby threatening the
integrity of elections. Further, they disenfranchise an
inordinate number of eligible Black voters and voters
of color. This was precisely what the NVRA is designed
to prevent.
Moreover, a federal consent decree here requires
Arizona to register eligible voters for federal elections
regardless of whether such voters use the state’s own
registration form or the form prescribed by the United
States Election Assistance Commission —even when
unaccompanied by documentary proof of citizenship.
That decree is a final judgment that binds the parties.
A State cannot evade or unilaterally nullify such a
decree by enacting a n allegedly  conflicting statute.
U.S. Const. Art. VI, cl. 2. Because the LULAC Decree
remains in force, principles of comity require the
courts below to give it effect. If the Petitioner wish es
to seek modification or vacatur of the decree, the
appropriate forum is the issuing court. This Court
should therefore affirm the decision below.
I. The NVRA Was Enacted to Foster
Participation by Reducing Barriers to
Voter Registration and to Ban Harmful
Voter Purges.
Prior to the enactment of the NVRA, restrictive
registration requirements and aggressive voter
purges—particularly purges implemented shortly
before an election—frequently disenfranchised eligible
voters. Often by design, such practices

7
disproportionately excluded  Black voters and other
voters of color, especially in jurisdictions with a
history of intentional discrimination. To remedy
unequal treatment and foster broad participation in
the democratic process, the NVRA bars states from
imposing registration requirements for federal
elections beyond the minimum amount necessary to
determine eligibility. With respect to voter purges,
among other restrictions, the NVRA prohibits
systematic removal of voters from the rolls within 90
days of a federal election and bans non -uniform or
discriminatory voter removal programs. S. Rep. No.
103-6, 103rd Cong., 1st Sess. (1993), 1993 WL 54278.
In enacting this legislation, Congress was acutely
aware that “discriminatory and unfair registration
laws … disproportionately harm voter participation by
various groups, including racial minorities.” 52 U.S.C.
§ 20501; see also S. Rep. No. 103-6, 1993 WL 54278, at
*2. Congress enacted the NVRA under its Elections
Clause authority to prevent restrictive registration
practices and regulate the timing and procedures for
removing ineligible voters from the registration rolls.
Today, burdensome registr ation procedures and
indiscriminate, inaccurate voter purges —under the
guise of preventing registration and voting by alleged
non-citizens—mirror the historical practices the
NVRA prohibits, disenfranchising eligible voters.
These burdens, including documentary proof of
citizenship and systematic purges within 90 days of a

8
federal election, violate the NVRA and subvert its
statutory purpose.
A. Before the NVRA, Registration Requirements
and Voter Purges Discriminated Against Black
Voters and Other Voters of Color.
Voter registration requirements were instituted in
the late 1800s in the South to disenfranchise Black
people and in the North and Midwest to disenfranchise
new immigrants. Steve Barber et al., The Purging of
Empowerment: Voter Purge Laws and the Voting
Rights Act , 23 Harv. C.R. -C.L. L. Rev. 483 (1988);
Danya L. Cunningham, Who Are to Be the Electors?, 9
Yale Law & Policy Rev. 370, 373 -74 (1991) (noting in
the South, the movement to shift registration burdens
to the electorate was an “explicitly white supremacist
drive to return the antebellum slavocracy to power”).
Among the voter registration practices used to
disenfranchise Black voters, the “discretion granted to
local officials to implement the various statutory
requirements and exemptions became the South’s
most powerful disfranchising tool.” Cunningham, 9
Yale Law & Policy Rev. at 380.
Even in the mid -twentieth century, particularly
after this Court’s decision in Brown, 347 U.S. 483,
onerous registration requirements kept Black people
off the voting rolls across the South, with voter purges
and mass challenges ejecting those who succeeded in
registering. In the mid -1950s, many parishes in
Louisiana amplified their use of the interpret ation

9
test, requiring prospective Black registrants to
interpret a constitutional provision to the registrar’s
satisfaction. Louisiana v. United States, 380 U.S. 145,
149 (1965). In response to Brown , the Louisiana
Legislature launched a joint legislative committee
called the “Segregation Committee.” Id.  Among other
things, the Committee initiated programs for parish
registrars to promote “white supremacy” and
advocated for “wholesale challeng[es to] Negro names
already on the voting rolls, with the result that
thousands of Negroes, but virtually no whites, were
purged from the rolls of voters.” Id. Voter purges thus
were a critical mechanism to prevent Black people
from exercising electoral influence and influencing
policy in the Southern states.  Barber, 23 Harv. C.R.-
C.L. L. Rev. at 487.
Using voter purges and mass challenges, Louisiana
disenfranchised almost the entire Black population in
some parishes. Citizen council groups challenged the
registration of Black voters under Louisiana law that
imposed identification requirements and requi red
voters to accurately complete unnecessarily complex
registration forms, resulting in mass purges from
voting lists. See , e.g., United States v. Lucky , 239 F.
Supp. 233, 236-37 (W.D. La. 1965) (enjoining a racially
discriminatory voter purge program); United States v.
Ass’n of Citizens Councils of La., Inc., 196 F. Supp. 908,
910-12 (W.D. La. 1961) (three -judge court) (same);
United States v. McElveen , 180 F. Supp. 10, 14 (E.D.
La. 1960) (three -judge court), aff’d in part sub nom.

10
United States v. Thomas, 362 U.S. 58 (1960) (same).
Many of these Black voters were challenged in the
weeks immediately preceding an election. For
example, in Grant Parish in 1956, where less than 800
Black voters were initially registered, “more than 700”
Black people were “pur ged 2 weeks before the
November general election,” and only “399 had cleared
the challenges a week before the deadline.” 85th Cong.
1st Sess. (July 26, 1957), at 12794
https://www.congress.gov/85/crecb
/1957/07/26/GPO-CRECB-1957-pt10-1-1.pdf.
Similarly, Ouachita Parish had some 4,000 registered
Black voters in the early fall of 1956, but a purge in
October prevented more than 3,000 of them from
voting in the general election on November 6. Id.  In
1956 and 1957, purges ousted around 11,000 Black
voters in just 12 parishes, with some parishes purging
ninety-nine percent of their Black voters. Barber , 23
Harv. C.R. -C.L. L. Rev. at 487; see also  Assn. of
Citizens Councils of La., Inc ., 196 F. Supp. at 9 10
(purging “approximately 95%” of all registered Black
voters and “less than 1%” of White voters in Bienville
Parish for the same registration errors).
The VRA did not eliminate this problem. In
Alabama, the Linden County registrar registered
voters only in the County Seat and for only two days a
month.  The Eleventh Circuit held that the obstacles
to registration created by these policies
“unquestionably discriminated against blacks.”
United States v. Marengo Cnty.  Comm’n, 731 F.2d

11
1546, 1570 (11th Cir. 1984). Likewise, in Dallas
County, the Eleventh Circuit determined that
evidence of ongoing discrimination against Black
voters supported a vote dilution claim, citing the
county registrar’s “limited hours, failure to go to the
beats to register voters, and refusal to appoint deputy
registrars.”  United States v. Dallas Cnty.  Comm’n,
739 F.2d 1529, 1538-39 (11th Cir. 1984).
During the same period, Mississippi employed a
dual registration system that made registration
unnecessarily cumbersome, particularly for rural
voters.  Miss. St. Chapter, Operation Push v. Allain,
674 F. Supp. 1245, 1249 (N.D. Miss. 1987), aff’d, 932
F.2d 400 (5th Cir. 1991). In some municipalities,
residents wishing to vote in county, state, and federal
elections, had to first register with the county
registrar or a deputy.  Id. Without such prior
registration at the inconvenient county offices, the
more accessible municipal clerks could only register
voters  for municipal elections. Id. Further impeding
registration, the State eliminated “satellite
registration” around each county, thus requiring
voters to register in person at the office of the county
registrar. Id. at 1251- 52. These labyrinthine
procedures disadvantaged Black residents so much
that Black voter registration dropped by nearly half
after their enactment and continued to be suppressed
well after the passage of the VRA. Id. at 1252-55.

12
Likewise in Georgia, a federal court in 1980 faulted
voter registration procedures for enabling arbitrary
decision-making on voter eligibility. See NAACP,
Dekalb Cnty. v. Georgia, 494 F.Supp. 668, 672 (N.D.
Ga. 1980) (policy of Dekalb County Board of Registrars
“concerning registration drive requests from
community groups may fairly be characterized as
erratic”).
As for purges, the Justice Department objected
repeatedly to voter purges throughout the 1980s. See ,
e.g., Letter from Wm. Bradford Reynolds, Assistant
Att’y Gen., DOJ Civ. Rts.  Div., to Floyd R. Cook,
Chairman, Perry Cnty. Comm’n , Ala. (Sep. 25, 1981),
https://www.justice.gov/sites/default/files/crt/legacy/2
014/05/30/AL-1450.pdf (objecting to purge and
reidentification of voters as “dilut[ing ] the voting
strength of the black electorate in Perry County”);
Letter from Wm. Bradford Reynolds, Assistant Att’y
Gen., DOJ Civ. Rts.  Div., to Lynda K. Oswald,
Assistant Att’y Gen., Ala. (Dec.  11, 1984),
https://www.justice.gov/sites/default/files/crt/legacy/2
014/05/30/AL-1640.pdf (objecting to purge and
reidentification of voters and noting “black voters …
may be particularly affected by the reidentification
process and the resulting voter purge ”); Letter from
John R. Dunne, Assistant Att’y Gen., DOJ Civ. Rts.
Div., to Debbie Barnes, Chairperson, Dallas Cnty. Bd.
of Registrars, Ala. (June 22, 1990)
https://www.justice.gov/sites/default/files/crt/legacy/2
014/05/30/AL-1800.pdf (objecting to implementation of

13
Alabama’s statewide voter reidentification and purge
law for causing “many black voters [to] believe[] they
were not qualified to vote in the June 5, 1990, primary
election”).
In 1982, Alabama law targeted only counties in the
state’s Black Belt for a total purge and reregistration
requirement. House Comm. on the Judiciary, Voting
Rights Act Extension, H.R. Rep. No. 227, 97th Cong.,
1st Sess. 16 (1981); Hearings Before the Subcomm. on
Civ. and Const. Rights of the House Comm. on the
Judiciary, Ser. No. 24, 97th Cong., 1st Sess. 830
(1981). Testifying before the House Judiciary
Committee, one Alabama Judge, Eddie Hardaway,
explained:
“[I]t is no accident that five of the seven
counties designated for re-registration in
1981 [were] in the ‘black belt.’ These re -
registration bills [were] passed by the
legislature as local legislation under
‘Gentlemen’s Agreements.’ The State
Representative of Perry County
[Alabama], in the black belt, won his last
election by 82 votes. The sponsor of the
Wilcox and Lowndes Counties' bill
exempted the predominantly white
counties in his district from compliance
with the registration bill.”
House Comm. on the Judiciary, H.R. Rep. No. 227,
97th Cong., 1st Sess. 16;  Hearings Before the

14
Subcomm. on Civ. and Const. Rts. of the House Comm.
on the Judiciary, Ser. No. 24, 97th Cong., 1st Sess. 830.
Other states similarly used voter purges and mass
challenges to eliminate Black voters from the rolls.
Subdivisions in Mississippi instituted voter purges
combined with re- registration requirements to
disadvantaged Black citizens. E.g. , Crowe v. Lucas,
472 F. Supp. 937 (N.D. Miss. 1979). Georgia’s practice
of removing registered voters from the registration list
when they missed elections faced a preclearance
objection for being “likely to have a disproportionate
adverse effect on minority voters in th e state.” Letter
from Deval L. Patrick, Assistant Att’y Gen., DOJ Civ.
Rts. Div., to Dennis R. Dunn, Senior Assistant Att’y
Gen., Ga. (Oct. 24, 1994),
https://www.justice.gov/sites/default/files/crt/legacy/2
014/05/30/GA-2570.pdf. And in South Carolina, local
registrars required voters to re-register each time they
moved and purged all voters who moved.
Cunningham, 9 Yale Law & Policy Rev. at 377 (citing
Steven F. Lawson, Black Ballots: Voting Rights in the
South, 1944-1969, at 6 (1976)). The Fifth Circuit
sitting en banc overturned a Louisiana city’s primary
election results where the registrar had selectively
“purg[ed] the voter rolls in a manner directed at black
voters but not at white voters.” Toney v. White , 488
F.2d 310, 312 (5th Cir. 1973) (en banc).
Unequal treatment of Black and other voters of
color extended beyond the South. For example,

15
Chicago’s voter purge system in the 1980s identified
Black voters and other voters of color as ineligible and
wrongfully purged them at twice the rate of White
voters. Barber, 23 Harv. C.R.-C.L. L. Rev. at 492-94.
In 1984, civil rights groups like LDF testified in
Congress about the significant barriers faced by Black
voters seeking to re-register once purged in Southern
states like Georgia. LDF attorney Lani Guinier
testified that around 1.5 million people, one third of
them Black, were not registered to vote in Georgia in
1984. Voting Rights Act: Runoff Primaries and
Registration Barriers: Hearings on the 1982
Amendment of the Voting Rights Act of 1965 Before
the Subcomm. on Civ. and Const. Rights of the House
Comm. on the Judiciary, 98th Cong., 2d Sess. 136
(1985), at 121 (testimony of Lani Guinier).
Thus, in considering the NVRA, Congress had a
wealth of testimony and information showing that
discriminatory registration requirements and
systematic voter purges disproportionately kept Black
citizens and other citizens  of color from voting. See
supra I.A. pp. 8-15; see generally Cunningham, 9 Yale
Law & Policy Rev. 370.

16
B. Congress Sought in the NVRA to Increase
Political Participation by Expanding
Registration Opportunities, Removing Barriers
to Registration, and Banning All Systematic
Voter Purges Near Federal Elections.
When it enacted the NVRA, Congress found that
“discriminatory and unfair registration laws and
procedures can have a direct and damaging effect on
voter participation in elections for Federal office and
disproportionately harm voter participation by
various groups, including racial minorities.” 52 U.S.C
§ 20501(a). This finding —which was a crucial reason
for the NVRA’s adoption —is well supported by the
historical evidence.
Despite the passage of the VRA, Black voter
participation in 1980 was 7 % below what it was in
1964, in large part because of voter purges and
burdensome re-registration requirements. Barber , 23
Harv. C.R. -C.L. L. Rev. at 489 -90 n.36, 36 ( citing
Bureau of the Census, Dep’t of Com., Stat. Abstract of
the U.S. , 1987, at 244) . In 1984, Black voter
registration nationally was 3.3% lower than
registration for White voters. Id.  at 490 n.36.  In
Mississippi, Black voter registration was
approximately 20% lower than White voter
registration. Id. In 1988, Congress was particularly
worried about the steadily declining participation

17
rate, noting that in the 1988 Presidential election,
voter turnout was just 50.15 percent. Id.2
Unsurprisingly, when Congress began to formulate
national legislation in the 1980s to address these
issues, racial disparities were center stage. For
example, a 1989 report from the Senate Committee on
Rules and Administration on a predecessor bill to the
NVRA emphasized testimony from Dr. Allan J.
Lichtman, a scholar in the field of electoral analysis,
that “a registered voter in a predominantly minority
election district has a 35 percent greater chance of
being purged than a registered voter in a
predominantly white district.” S. Rep. 101-140, 101st
Cong., 1 st Sess. 1989, HeinOnline.  In this early
iteration of the NVRA , the Committee emphasized
that in requiring state programs to confirm lawful
registration “be uniform and non-discriminatory,” the
proposed statutory language was “intended to include
in the meaning that the procedure shall not
disproportionately remove minority or disabled voters
from the official list of registered voters.” Id.
In the Committee on House Administration’s 1993
report on H.R. 2, which ultimately became the NVRA,
the legislative findings explained that “restrictive
registration laws and administrative procedures were

2 Even in 1991, some 47% of eligible voters nationally were
unregistered, and that percentage was substantially higher for
Black voters and other voters of color. Cunningham, 9 Yale Law
& Policy Rev. at 385.

18
introduced in the United States in the late nineteenth
and early twentieth centuries to keep certain groups
of citizens from voting; in the North,” it was “the wave
of immigrants pouring into the industrial cities; in the
South, blacks and the rural poor.” H.R. Rep. No. 103-
9, 1st Sess. (1993) , 1993 WL 27395, at *2. These
restrictions were remarkably effective: “between 1896
and 1924, the voter turnout for Presidential elections
dropped from 79 percent to 49 percent.” Id. In the
South, the turnout dropped from 57 percent to 19
percent, with Black voter participation dropping from
44 percent to essentially zero. Id. These findings noted
that “the poll tax, literacy tests, residency
requirements, selective purges, elaborate
administrative procedures and annual reregistration
requirements were some of the techniques developed
to discourage participation.” Id.
The Senate emphasized the balance the legislation
intended to strike between addressing potential voter
fraud and preventing the large -scale removal of
eligible Black voters and other voters of color from the
rolls under the guise of addressing fraud. The Senate
Rules Committee Report stated that while “[t]he
maintenance of accurate and up -to-date voter
registration lists is the hallmark of a national system
seeking to prevent voter fraud … [s]uch  processes
must be structured to prevent abuse which has a
disparate impact on minority communities.” S. Rep.
No. 103-6, 1993 WL 54278, at *18.

19
By instituting requirements that purge programs
be “uniform, non- discriminatory” and completed at
least 90 days before a federal election, the NVRA
sought to increase federal election turnout and
prevent further discriminatory or inaccurate voter
removal. Specifically, with respect to the 90 -day and
“uniform, non- discriminatory” provisions of the Act,
the Senate Rules Committee Report notes that the
NVRA was designed “to prevent the discriminatory
nature of periodic voter purges, which … appear to
affect blacks and minorities more than others.” Id. at
*18, 20.
Congress was aware that mass voter roll purges
were instituted to disenfranchise immigrants, Black
people, and the rural poor, while also recognizing that
routine list maintenance is a hallmark of a fair
electoral system that guards against fraud. The 90 -
day provision and the requirement that, outside of
that window, purge programs be uniform and nondiscriminatory, were crucial to the balance Congress
struck to advance these dual goals of the NVRA.
Lastly, the NVRA’s legislative history is clear that
Congress intended to eliminate systematic barriers to
registration for eligible citizens. To paraphrase
Senator Wendell Ford, the sponsor of the legislation,
whether someone votes Republican, Democratic,  or
Independent “is not the point.” 103rd Congress, 1st
Sess. (Mar. 4, 1993), at 4210. What matters is that all

20
people “find it easy to register to vote”—and that they
stay registered so long as they stay eligible. Id.
The NVRA sought to protect voting as a
fundamental right—“not a prize reserved for those
who demonstrate the stamina and endurance to
overcome obstacles to register.” Id . at 4203.
Documentary proof of citizenship requirements and
purges aimed at removing alleged non -citizens before
a federal election raise exactly the kind of barrier s to
registration and voting  that Congress sought to
eliminate with the NVRA —unnecessary, unduly
restrictive, and disproportionately harmful to voters of
color.
C. Requiring Documentary Proof of Citizenship to
Register Contravenes the Text of the NVRA and
Congress’s Purpose in Adopting It.
The NVRA prescribes a Federal Form for
registration to vote in federal elections, but allows
states to devise their own registration forms, 52 U.S.C.
§ 20505(a)(2), to  promote equal access to voter
registration and thus, the ballot box . However , the
NVRA mandates that when States “develop and use”
their own voter registration forms, id. , for federal
elections, those forms “may require only such
identifying information … as is necessary to enable
the appropriate State election official to assess the
eligibility of the applicant.” 52 U.S.C. § 20508(b)(1).
Regarding the requirement of United States
citizenship, the NVRA spells out the information

21
Congress deem s necessary: The Act requires voter
registration forms for federal elections to include an
attestation under penalty of perjury that the applicant
is a citizen. Id.  § 20508(b)(2). The NVRA treats this
attestation as sufficient to verify the registrant’s
citizenship. Documentary proof of citizenship thus
goes beyond what is “necessary to ... assess []
eligibility” to vote in federal elections, a conclusion
that this Court has affirmed. See ITCA, 570 U.S. at 2.
In fact, Congress considered allowing States to require
DPOC for all registrations to vote in federal elections.
The Senate version of the bill included such a
provision.  The House bill did not. The Conference
Committee sided with the House, finding that the
provision allowing states to demand DPOC is “not
necessary or consistent with the purpose of this Act.”
H.R. Conf. Rep. No. 103-66, 1st Sess. (1993), 1993 WL
235764, at * 23.  Congress thus made a considered
judgment that the attestation under penalty of perjury
suffices to verify citizenship. To nevertheless require
proof of citizenship thwarts the NVRA’s stated
objectives by erecting needless  barriers to registering
for and voting in federal elections and by making
participation more difficult for eligible citizens.
The Help America Vote Act  (“HAVA”), enacted in
2002, imposed new proof of address and identification
requirements for voters registering by mail, but did
not require documentary proof of citizenship. 52
U.S.C. § 21083(b). Rather, Congress particularized the
requirements of the NVRA, requiring mail

22
registration forms to include specific language and
requiring registrants to affirm their citizenship simply
by checking a box. Id.  § 21083(b)(4). HAVA thus
reaffirms that Congress understood an affirmation of
citizenship under penalty of perjury to be all that was
necessary for a voter to prove citizenship. Yet u nder
laws like Arizona’s H.B. 2492, eligible citizens who are
unable to obtain documentary proof of citizenship will
be denied access to the democratic process. 2022 Ariz.
Sess. Laws, ch. 99 (“H.B. 2942”).
According to a national survey published in 2024,
21.3 million voting -age American citizens lack access
to a birth certificate, U.S. passport, or naturalization
papers. See Brennan Ctr., Millions of Americans Don’t
Have Documents Proving Their Citizenship Readily
Available (June 11, 2024),
https://www.brennancenter.org/our-work/analysisopinion/millions-americans-dont-have-documentsproving-their-citizenship-readily. Another 3.8 million
voting-age American citizens of voting age lack any
documents proving citizenship. Id. And this access gap
is particularly stark for, and disproportionately
affects, Black Americans and other people of color. Id.
Moreover, Black Americans and other Americans
of color are less likely than White Americans to
possess proof of citizenship documents.  Two-thirds of
Black Americans do not have a passport. Brennan
Ctr., House Bill Would Hurt American Voters (Jan. 14,
2025), www.brennancenter.org/our -work/analysis-

23
opinion/house-bill-would-hurt-american-voters. Non-
White Americans also are less likely than  White
Americans to have birth certificates, in part due to
historical discrimination. At the time of the 1940 U.S.
Census, 92% of White births were registered, whereas
82% of non-White births were registered. See Susan J.
Pearson, Ph.D., Comment to the U.S. Election
Assistance Commission, (“Pearson EAC Comment”) at
3 (2025) (citing Sam Shapiro, Recent Testing of Birth
Registration Completeness in the United States, 8
Population Stud. 15 -16 (1954)). In 1950, non- White
birth registration was 93.5%, compared to 98.6% for
White births. Id . A major predictor of birth
registration was whether the baby was born in a
hospital or at home. Id. In 1940-1950, states could, and
did, bar Black Americans from accessing private or
public hospitals, leading to more at -home births for
Black Americans and thus fewer birth registrations.
Id. Applicants seeking a delayed birth certificate face
extensive documentation, fees that are up to double or
triple the amount of an original certificate, and
discretionary denials if the evidence is deemed
unsatisfactory. See Susan Pearson, Ph.D., The Birth
Certificate: An American History , UNC Press (2021),
at 251–54; see also Pearson EAC Comment, at 5.  For
those unregistered or with delayed registration,
requiring documentary proof of citizenship to register
could deny them the right to vote.

24
D. Purges Purportedly Targeting Non-Citizens
During the Quiet Period Before an Election
Inaccurately Flag or Remove Black Voters in
Violation of the NVRA and in Derogation of Its
Purpose.
Today, despite Congress’s determination that voter
purges require regulation to prevent their
discriminatory impact, state s continue to implement
error-prone programs that disproportionately
disenfranchise Black voters and other voters of color.
For example, in 2024, the State of Alabama
admitted, and a federal court found, that Alabama
wrongly labeled over 2,000 voters as ineligible
noncitizens (out of just 3,251 identified voters). Not
only had Alabama erroneously declared these citizens
ineligible to vote, but based on its mislabeling of them
as non- citizens, it referred them for criminal
investigation. See Mot. Hr’g  Tr. 10/15 Doc. 92 at
134:12-137:17; Mot. Hr’g Tr. 10/16, Doc. 91 at 12:15-
14:13; Ala. Coal. for Immigrant Just . v. Allen , No.
2:24-cv-01254 (N.D. Ala. Oct. 16, 2024) , ECF No. 90.
In that case, expert evidence demonstrated that
Alabama’s citizenship -based voter purge effort
“incorrectly and disproportionately identifies racial
and ethnic minorities who are naturalized.” Ala. Coal.
for Immigrant Just. v. Allen, No. 2:24-cv-01254 (N.D.
Ala. Oct. 11, 2024) , ECF No. 74 -1 ¶ 118. In a similar
case, the Eastern District of  Virginia enjoined
Virginia’s parallel overly expansive attempt to purge
purported non-citizens from their voter rolls within 90

25
days of the 2024 election. Virginia Coal. for Immigrant
Rts. v. Beals, No. 1:24 -cv-01788, 2024 WL 4577983
(E.D. Va. Oct. 25, 2024), stayed , 2024 WL 4608863
(Mem).
And just two months ago, well within 90 days of the
upcoming 2026 federal elections, the Department of
Homeland Security claimed to have identified nearly
16,000 non- citizens on the voter rolls in Nevada
through unspecified database matching. See  Nick
Corasanti, “From 16,000 to 185 to Zero: Trump’s
Claims of Illegal Voting in Nevada Fizzle,”  New York
Times (Sep. 24, 2026). Of those alleged non- citizens,
the Department was able to provide Nevada election
officials with details on only 185 individuals. Id. After
the State investigated, all 185 proved to be eligible
citizens who would have been denied the right to vote
this year had Nevada acted on the Department’s
demands. Id.
And in 2012, a similar program in Florida
disproportionally flagged eligible Black voters as
noncitizens for removal from the voting rolls within 90
days of a federal election. Arcia v. Florida Sec 'y of
State, 772 F.3d 1335, 1348 (11th Cir. 2014). In Arcia,
one expert found that both the 180,000 voters initially
identified as “potential noncitizens” and the final list
of 2,625 registered voters targeted by the Florida
Secretary of State were largely eligible voters who
were disproportionately more likely to be racial and
ethnic minorities —with Black voters particularly

26
overrepresented.  Arcia v. Detzner, No. 1:12 -cv-22282
(S.D. Fla. Sep. 24, 2012), ECF No. 76-1. And the State
of Texas reached a settlement agreement with private
civil rights groups after its similar purge program
targeted tens of thousands of naturalized citizens, a
disproportionate share of whom were voters of color.
Texas LULAC v. Whitley, No. SA-19-CA-074-FB (W.D.
Tex. Apr. 26, 2019).
These examples highlight the unreliability of
systematic voter purge  programs, whether based on
citizenship or some other disqualifying characteristic,
which pose a particular  risk to  lawfully registered
Black voters and other voters of color . Congress
enacted the 90-day provision to avoid precisely these
results.
II. Principles of Comity Required the
Courts Below to Give Effect to a
Federal Consent Decree That Binds
Arizona Unless and Until Vacated or
Modified by the Issuing Court.
Petitioner and the United States ask this Court to
reverse the Ninth Circuit’s ruling that the consent
decree entered in League of United Latin American
Citizens of Arizona v. Reagan bars county clerks from
rejecting state form applicants who lack documentary
evidence of citizenship. RNC Br. at 34-39; U.S. Br. at
24-30; see No. 2:17-cv-4102 (D. Ariz.  June 18, 2018),
ECF No. 37 (“ LULAC Decree” or “Decree”). They do
not contest the Ninth Circuit’s conclusion that the

27
DPOC provisions of H.B. 2492 conflict with the
LULAC Decree. Instead, they urge various equitable
grounds for disregarding the Decree. None of their
arguments would permit the courts below to nullify
the final judgment of another federal court. And in any
event, the appropriate course for addressing any
inequity in the ongoing enforcement of the LULAC
Decree would be to seek relief from the judgment in
the original court. See Fed. R. Civ. P. 60(b).
The LULAC Decree, which instructs county
recorders to register eligible voters using the state
form for federal elections—even when unaccompanied
by documentary proof of citizenship —is a final
judgment that binds its parties. The State cannot
evade or unilaterally nullify that decree merely by
enacting a state statute that conflicts with it. U.S.
Const. Art. VI, cl. 2. Neither the State’s assertion that
the D ecree was consistent with state law  nor the
absence of explicit findings of a violation of federal law
alters the analysis. Because the Decree remains in
force, principles of comity required the courts below to
give it effect and preclude a collateral attack on it. The
appropriate forum in which to seek modification or
vacatur of the decree is the issuing court.
A. Consent Decrees Are a Crucial Tool to Protect
Civil Rights.
Consent decrees commonly override state law or
practice, especially when states are alleged to have
violated federal civil rights protections. Such decrees

28
are often the only practical avenue for Black people
and other people of color to vindicate their rights.
In the voting rights context, consent decrees have
routinely displaced state laws in the interest of
protecting federally guaranteed rights. For example,
during the COVID -19 pandemic, multiple states
agreed to consent decrees suspending state -law
requirements governing mail balloting and other
matters. Thus, in pandemic- era Rhode Island, a
federal district court approved a consent decree under
which the Secretary of State and other state officials
agreed to suspend the two- witness or notary
attestation rule  for voting by mail.  Common Cause
Rhode Island v. Gorbea , No. 1:20 -cv-00318, 2020 WL
4460914, at *4 (D.R.I. July 30, 2020). This Court
declined to stay that injunction, noting that where
state officials “support the challenged decree,” third
parties “lack a cognizable interest in the State’s ability
to enforce its duly enacted laws .” Republican Nat’l
Comm. v. Common Cause Rhode Island, 591 U.S. 1074
(2020) (Mem) (cleaned up); see also  League of Women
Voters of Virginia v. Virginia State Bd. of Elections,
458 F. Supp. 3d 442, 446 (W.D. Va. 2020) (similar).
In an earlier era, the Dillard litigation of the 1980s
produced consent decrees that displaced existing
election systems throughout Alabama. Twenty years
after the enactment of the Voting Rights Act, dozens
of Alabama municipalities, county commissions, and
school boards throughout the state’s Black Belt

29
maintained at -large systems of election and other
discriminatory devices for the express purpose of
keeping political power out of the hands of the Black
citizens who made up a majority of their populations.
James Blacksher et. al., Voting Rights in Alabam a:
1982-2006, 17 S. C AL. REV. L. & Soc. Just. 249, 260
(2008) (collecting cases); see also Dillard v. Crenshaw
Cnty., 640 F. Supp. 1347, 1357 (M.D. Ala. 1986) (citing
statements defending numbered place laws and other
rules “to protect the white people of Alabama” from
Black voters’ purported illiteracy, “criminal records,
[and] criminal attitudes ”). Litigation throughout the
region resulted in consent decrees that altered these
systems in ways not contemplated by state law. E.g. ,
Dillard v. Town of Cuba , 708 F. Supp. 1244, 1245
(M.D. Ala. 1988) (approving consent decree adopting a
“limited voting” system for city council elections).
Ultimately, after these alternative systems of election
were codified in state law and precleared by the
Attorney General, many were dissolved. E.g.,  Dillard
v. Crenshaw Cnty., No. CIV.A.2:85CV1332-MHT, 2006
WL 3392071 (M.D. Ala. July 31, 2006) (dissolving the
Dillard consent decree pertaining to Calhoun County
citing Alabama Act No. 2006– 252, known as the
Dillard Act, codified at Ala. Code § 11-80-12 (2006); see
also Ala. Code § 11 -3-1(c) (2008) (broadening the
Dillard Act)).
Consent decrees remain a powerful tool to
vindicate federally protected civil rights. In 2024, a
consent decree settled the Braxton v. Stokes litigation

30
simply by requiring an Alabama city to hold mayoral
elections and provide the public notice of them.
Braxton v. Town of Newbern , No. 2:23-CV-00127-KD-
N, 2024 WL 3519193, at *1 (S.D. Ala. July 23, 2024 ).
Before entering into the consent agreement, the City
of Newbern had not held a mayoral election since
1965. Instead, it had passed down the role of mayor for
decades, almost exclusively to White residents and
without public input or consent. Alaizah Koorji,
Defending Consent Decrees in the Wake of Horne v.
Flores, Harv. L. Rev. Blog (Nov. 13, 2024).
B. A Mere Change in State Law Does Not Nullify
or Require Modification of an Institutional
Reform Consent Decree.
The LULAC Decree is a final judgment and “an
agreement that the parties desire and expect will be
reflected in, and be enforceable as, a judicial decree
that is subject to the rules generally applicable to
other judgments and decrees.” Rufo v. Inmates of
Suffolk Cnty. Jail , 502 U.S. 367, 378, 391 (1992).
Lower courts have long recognized consent decrees as
enforceable and final. See, e.g., Washington v. Penwell,
700 F.2d 570, 574 (9th Cir. 1983) (“ That compliance
with a decree enforcing federal law will have an
ancillary effect on the state treasury is the inevitable
and permissible consequence of Ex parte Young -type
suits.”); United States v. Kellum, 523 F.2d 1284, 1287
(5th Cir. 1975) (collecting cases).

31
Like other judgments, consent decrees are subject
to modification or vacatur under Rule 60(b)(5).
Modification or vacatur of a final judgment is the
exception, not the rule. Such relief may be appropriate
where “a significant change in circumstances” renders
continued enforcement inequitable, Rufo, 502 U.S. at
383, or “when the objects of the decree have been
attained,” Frew ex rel. Frew v. Hawkins, 540 U.S. 431,
442 (2004). Courts consider modifying or vacating a
consent decree “only to the extent that equity
requires.” Rufo, 502 U.S. at 391. Where circumstances
have changed sufficiently to warrant relief under Rule
60(b)(5), any modification must be “suitably tailored to
the changed circumstance.” Id.
A significant change in facts or in law may justify
revision of a consent decree. Thus, a “consent decree
must of course be modified if, as it later turns out, one
or more of the obligations placed upon the parties has
become impermissible under federal  law.” Id. at 388
(emphasis added). In an institutional reform case,
however, a mere clarification of federal law may not
warrant modifying a consent decree so long as its
obligations remain permissible and consistent with
the underlying federal rights. Id.  at 389 (“[A]
clarification in the law [does not] automatically open[]
the door for relitigation of the merits of every affected
consent decree”). In Rufo, for example, this Court held
that a prison reform consent decree need not be
modified merely because a later decision clarified that

32
its obligations exceeded the constitutional minimum.
Id. at 388-89.
That is especially true where, as here, the claims
underlying a consent decree are not at issue  in the
subsequent dispute. The LULAC Decree rested on
claims under the First and Fourteenth Amendments
to the U.S. Constitution , not the NVRA . Consent
Decree at 1-2. Thus, any clarification concerning the
State’s obligations under the NVRA would have no
bearing on the basis for the consent decree. Moreover,
even if this Court were to hold that the Constitution
and the NVRA permit states to require documentary
evidence of citizenship, registering federal voters
without such evidence would remain  lawful under
federal law. Indeed, the majority of  states implement
the mandates of the NVRA without imposing a DPOC
requirement.3 Treating state -form registrations the
same as federal -form registrants, as the LULAC
Decree requires, is thus a reasonable means of
complying with NVRA. In other words, “[t]he decree
reflects a choice among various ways that a State could
implement the [NVRA].” Frew , 540 U.S. at 439.
Accordingly, no decision from this Court could require

3 Nor can it be argued that there was any “misunderstanding” as
to what federal law required at the time the LULAC Decree was
negotiated, as Petitioner contends. RNC Br. at 36. In the LULAC
Decree, the Secretary maintained her position that the state’s
DPOC requirement was permissible under the Constitution, even
as applied to state-form registrants registering to vote in federal
elections. LULAC Decree, at 4. She simply chose to compromise
that position.

33
a modification of the LULAC Decree. Id. at 438- 39
(rejecting the argument that enforcement of a consent
decree requires a showing that the violation of the
decree also violates the underlying federal law).
Arizona’s adoption of H.B. 2492 does not amount to
a change in circumstance that fatally undermines the
Decree. Petitioner’ s contrary argument relies on
instances in which a change in federal —not state —
law substantially altered the circumstances that
justified an earlier decree. See  Rufo, 502 U.S. at 388-
89 (examining whether this Court’s decision in Bell v.
Wolfish, 441 U.S. 520 (1979) required re -examination
of a prison conditions consent decree); Sys. Fed. No. 91,
Ry. Emps.’ v. Wright , 364 U.S. 642, 650- 51 (1961)
(holding that a change to the federal Railway Labor
Act required modification of a consent decree);
Agostini v. Felton , 521 U.S. 203, 222 (1997)
(overturning this Court’s precedent established in the
same case and vacating permanent injunction).
Standing alone, a change in state law does not and
cannot supersede a federal consent decree. Since the
time of Chief Justice John Marshall, it has been
axiomatic that a state’s legislature may not “annul the
judgments of the courts of the United States, a nd
destroy the rights acquired under those judgments.”
Cooper v. Aaron, 358 U.S. 1, 18 (1958) (quoting United
States v. Peters, 9 U.S. 115, 136 (1809)). The
Supremacy Clause requires a state to comply with
judgments and orders of the federal judiciary—in this

34
case, the LULAC Decree—and any state law to the
contrary must give way. See  U.S. Const. Art VI, cl. 2;
Cooper, 358 U.S. at 18-19.
It makes no difference to the enforceability of the
LULAC court’s final judgment that state law now
prohibits what was allegedly permitted at the time the
Decree was entered. Indeed, the express purpose of
H.B. 2492 to thwart the LULAC Decree is a compelling
reason not to modify it. Frew , 540 U.S. at 442
(modification or dissolution of a consent decree
appropriate “when the objects of the decree have been
attained”); see also O’Sullivan v. City of Chicago , 396
F.3d 843, 865 (7th Cir. 2005) (changes to a consent
decree’s legal or factual premises do not justify
“ignoring or defying the decree”). Nor is it of any
moment that the Secretary’s consent rested on the
premise that the actions required by the LULAC
Decree were purportedly permissible under state law.
Once that consent was transformed into a final
judgment, it bound the parties to its terms.
C. The Appropriate Venue for Seeking
Modification of the LULAC Decree Is the
Issuing Court.
Even if the enactment of H.B. 2492 were grounds
for seeking a modification of the LULAC  Decree, the
suggestion that the lower courts should have
disregarded the Decree is misplaced. Rule 60(b)
provides the mechanism by which a party or interested
non-party may seek relief from a judgment. Fed. R.

35
Civ. P. 60(b); Horne v Flores , 557 U.S. 433 (2009)
(permitting intervention of state legislative leaders for
the purpose of seeking relief under Rule 60(b)(5)) .
Under that rule, a court may modify its own decree
when equity so requires. Frew, 540 U.S. at 441; Rufo ,
502 U.S. at 383.  That relief must be sought in the
proceeding in which the judgment was entered. 12
Moore's Fed. Prac. § 60.02 (3d ed. 2024); 7 Moore's Fed.
Pract. § 60.19 (3d ed. 2015); see also Brown v.
McCormick, 608 F.2d 410, 413 (10th Cir. 1979).
Indeed, Petitioner RNC seems to concede as much.
RNC Br. at 35 (“the issuing court  must consider
‘changing circumstances’”).
Petitioner and the United States  suggest that the
Respondents inappropriately commandeered these
collateral proceedings to enforce the consent decree.
RNC Br. 40-41; U.S. Br. 25. This argument turns Rule
60(b)(5) on its head. It is the party seeking relief from
a judgment that bears the burden of establishing
changed circumstances. In this case, it is Petitioner
who seek s modification or vacatur of the LULAC
Decree. As such, it was incumbent upon them to seek
that relief in the appropriate venue.
The United States erroneously relies on this
Court’s decision in Martin v. Wilks, 490 U.S. 755, 768-
69 (1989), to argue that Petitioner ’s collateral attack
on the LULAC Decree in this proceeding is proper.
Wilks is inapposite. Wilks did not address whether
collateral litigation could be used to undo or modify an
